questions.q: What is the key practical difference between `functools.lru_cache` and `diskcache`?
options: lru_cache only works with strings, while diskcache works with any data type
lru_cache stores results in the current process's memory and loses them when the process exits; diskcache persists results to disk so they survive across process restarts
diskcache is always slower than lru_cache in every scenario
lru_cache requires a database server to run
questions.explain: lru_cache's cache lives in process memory and disappears on exit; diskcache writes to disk, so a cache built up in one script run or job is still available the next time the process starts, which matters for research pipelines run repeatedly over time.

questions.q: Why is cache invalidation described as one of the genuinely hard problems in caching?
options: Because caches automatically delete themselves after 24 hours

Because the cache key must capture everything that actually determines the output -- too loose a key causes stale wrong answers to be returned for genuinely different inputs, while too specific a key never hits
Because disk space is always too limited to store a cache
Because Python does not support dictionaries larger than 1000 entries
questions.explain: The core difficulty is correctness, not performance: a cache key that omits an argument that actually affects the result (e.g. keying only on signal_name while lookback also matters) causes two different calls to collide and the second to wrongly reuse the first's stale answer.

questions.q: In the `expensive_backtest` example, why does the third call (different `lookback`) take about 1.004s again instead of returning instantly like the second call?
options: diskcache has a maximum of two cached entries
The cache key includes lookback, and a different lookback value produces a different key, so it is correctly treated as a new computation rather than reusing the first call's cached result
The third call always re-runs regardless of the cache
time.sleep() ignores cached results
questions.explain: The cache key is (signal_name, lookback) -- both values that actually determine the result -- so changing lookback produces a genuinely different key, correctly causing a cache miss and a fresh computation rather than reusing a stale cached answer.

questions.q: What does the real measured timing in this lesson's example demonstrate?
options: That diskcache is incompatible with time.sleep()
That the second call with identical arguments returned in about 0.000s versus 1.004s for the first call, directly proving the cache avoided redoing the expensive computation
That the first call is always faster than later calls
That caching only works for integer return values
questions.explain: The measured timing is the actual evidence: a 1.004s first call followed by a ~0.000s second call with identical arguments confirms the cache hit skipped the simulated expensive work rather than merely claiming it would.

questions.q: According to the lesson's closing section, how does caching fit into the overall research pipeline built across this chapter?
options: It replaces the need for a data layer entirely

It is one more piece of the same reproducibility and efficiency story -- wrapping expensive computation steps so a scheduled job or re-run after a crash doesn't redo finished work, alongside the data layer's own caching and DuckDB's columnar efficiency
It only matters for kdb+-based systems
It is unrelated to the data layer or scheduled jobs covered earlier in the course
questions.explain: The lesson frames caching as integrating with the data layer (lesson 25), scheduled jobs (lesson 27), and columnar SQL access (lessons 28-29) into one coherent pipeline, rather than as an isolated optimization trick bolted on at the end.
